objectives: Use compass circles to find endpoints consistent with triangle side lengths.
Explain by hinged strips when triangle length conditions are impossible.
Reason about strict third-side bounds using repeated concrete examples.

studentActivityComparison.source: Slide lies 5 m east of swings. Lin is 3 m from slide; many possible placements on a circle.
studentActivityComparison.implementation: Existing Rich V2 does not offer this metric park-location opening. New diagram teaches the same endpoint-locus structure using triangle lengths, but 7.1 as such remains UNVERIFIED_SOURCE_TASK_PARITY.

studentActivityComparison.activity: 7.2 How Long Is the Third Side?
studentActivityComparison.source: Construct many triangles with fixed sides 5 and 4 inches, including third lengths beyond and outside slider settings; optional 9 and 5 inch extensions.
studentActivityComparison.implementation: Original asset explicitly states 1 < third side < 9 inches for 5 and 4, and grade-owned source check covers endpoints. Physical slider/user submitted set is NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

studentActivityComparison.source: Trace a 3-inch rotating side; use two 3-inch endpoint circles with a 4-inch base; intersection constructs triangle; consider all endpoint choices.
studentActivityComparison.implementation: Original SVG has radius-3 circles at opposite ends of 4-inch base, two mirrored intersections, both congruent 4-3-3 triangles; distinguishes mirror copies from different triangle sizes.

studentActivityComparison.source: For base 21 units and hinge radii 4 and 2, circles cannot meet; explain why shorter segments cannot reach.
studentActivityComparison.implementation: Second original SVG panel draws exact base/radii in a separate scale and verifies a 15-unit separation gap. Still requires learner construction or manipulatives, not merely looking at a picture.

studentOriginalConstruction: Use a compass to draw circles of 3-inch radius from both ends of a 4-inch base. Mark both intersections and draw both triangles; explain why reflection gives identical shape despite changed orientation. Use two circles of radii 4 and 2 inches on a 21-inch base, explain why there are no intersections, and physically explore strictly valid third sides for a 5- and 4-inch pair. Submit sketches and written explanation for teacher review.

criteria.description: Draw a correctly measured 4-inch base and two 3-inch radius endpoint circles; mark both intersections and accurately construct corresponding triangles.
Explain why the two reflected triangle constructions are congruent, not different side-length solutions; identify repeated base/arc lengths.
Use measured strips or circles to show 21/4/2 cannot close and that a 5/4 third side must lie strictly between 1 and 9 inches.
Present original measured diagrams, correct units and a mathematical justification, including why boundary values are degenerate.

teacherRubricDraft.scoring: Teacher must inspect physical or digital learner constructions and explanations; no automatic numeric credit.

cases.claim: Two intersections of r=3 circles with base=4 yield mirrored congruent triangles; 21/4/2 has no intersection; 1<x<9 for 5/4.
cases.outcome: Correct mathematical description; teacher construction/reasoning still unverified.

cases.claim: For 21/4/2 circles meet because 4+2 is positive.
cases.outcome: Reject; 4+2=6 <21, center distance exceeds radius sum.

cases.claim: Upper and lower 4/3/3 constructions make noncongruent triangles.
cases.outcome: Reject; reflection preserves lengths and angles.

cases.claim: Third side =9 or =1 with fixed 5 and4 produces a triangle.
cases.outcome: Reject; circles tangent/collinear, no nondegenerate triangle.

cases.claim: A single given 4-inch base and a 3-inch side alone determine the third vertex uniquely.
cases.outcome: Reject; free endpoint traces circle, additional condition is needed.

cases.claim: Writes the bounds with no circle or strip construction or explanation.
Uses different compass radii without labels or counts two circles as two sides.
